chapter: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
title: Don Byas: advanced harmony, small stature and scraps
summary: Byas sat in with Tatum and played Minton's; Stewart describes him as short but powerful, half humble and half cocky, who got into fights.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: Well, you know, one of the things that comes out very clear in that is that Mr. Byas harmonically was
Yes, he was. Oh, my goodness, yes.
He was -- did you work much with him, other than in that situation?
You mentioned earlier that he sat in -- he's one of the few people that sat in with the Tatum
Yes, he sat in with us while I was with Tatum at the Three Deuces and lots of occasions, I had a chance to play with Don, you know, even up at the Minton's Playhouse, you know.
Oh, he was one of the guys, too, that would go up there.
When the guys were working out the bebop stuff, he's one of the guys up there.
What kind of a guy was Byas? He was a very small man.
He was short, little man, you might say. But he had some, you might say, some powerful chops, you know, with that saxophone. It was beautiful.
Did you find him -- was he like a humble guy or a arrogant guy or a cocky guy or --
I think it was half and half, yeah. At

times, I couldn't -- I'd seen him get into a few hassles on 52nd Street and on other occasions, it was real cool, you know. But don't make him angry, you know. Just one of those things, you know. Yeah, I've seen him get into some scraps, you know.

Well, not other musicians. Maybe once or twice, he might have had an argument, a light argument with another musician. I've seen him get into arguments with, you might say, a sailor or something like that, even walking down the street during the war years, you know.
